hero.title: Kolabr vs Slack
hero.lede: Working with clients in Slack carries two bills: the guests who need a second channel and become billable members, and the tracker and the knowledge base you bought to stand beside it. Kolabr charges for your team and nobody else, in any number of channels, with requests, a wiki and scheduled events already in the price. Here are the two side by side on guest cost, accountability, knowledge and price.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: Kolabr does everything you use Slack for, then adds the parts you currently bolt on: requests with owners and deadlines, a wiki in every channel, and scheduled events. Guests are free wherever you put them, so you stop rationing who gets invited.

summary.title: The number that decides it
summary.body: Twelve people and forty client contacts who each need more than one channel: $120 a month on Kolabr Pro, $455 on Slack Pro. The gap is not the seat price, it is everyone who is not staff.

statement.title: The second channel is where it gets expensive
paragraphs: Slack gives you free guests on one condition: one channel each, and no more than five for every paid member. It holds up while a client only ever needs a single room. It stops holding up the moment the same client has a project channel, a billing question and a support thread, because that person is now a multi-channel guest and is charged at your full seat rate.

Kolabr has one kind of guest. Free, in as many channels as the work requires, with no allowance to track and nothing that converts them into a paid seat later. The practical result is that you stop deciding who is worth inviting, and the people with the answers are simply in the room.

items.title: Are Slack guests free?
items.body: A single-channel guest is free, and you may have up to five of them for every paid active member. The moment that person needs a second channel they become a multi-channel guest and are billed at your full per-seat rate. So the honest answer is that guests are free while one channel is genuinely enough. In Kolabr a guest is free in any number of channels, with no allowance to count and no upgrade to trip over.

items.title: What is the difference between Slack Connect and a guest?
items.body: Slack Connect links a channel between two Slack workspaces, so each person stays in their own account under their own policies. It works well, with one condition: both organisations need a paid Slack plan. A client who does not use Slack, or uses the free plan, falls back to being a guest in your workspace. Kolabr has no equivalent condition, because a guest only needs an email address.

items.title: Is Kolabr cheaper than Slack?
items.body: For almost anyone working with clients, yes, and the gap widens as you take more on. A twelve-person agency with forty client contacts pays $120 a month on Kolabr Pro. The same people on Slack Pro are fifty-two billable members at $8.75, which is $455. Per internal seat the two are close, $10 against $8.75 monthly. The difference is everyone who is not staff: in Slack a guest who needs a second channel becomes a full member, and in Kolabr guests are free in as many channels as the work needs.

items.title: Can Kolabr replace Slack entirely?
items.body: Yes, and most customers end up there. Kolabr runs internal team channels, private and group messages, calls and file sharing the same way it runs client channels. What it adds is the layer Slack leaves to other products: requests with owners and deadlines, a wiki in each channel, and scheduled events tied to the work they belong to.

items.title: What does Kolabr do that Slack does not?
items.body: Requests with a category, an owner and a response-time target the client can see. A wiki that lives in the channel and stays readable to guests. Scheduled events tied to the request that caused them. And unlimited free guests, which changes how many people you are willing to invite into the room.

items.title: We already have years of history in Slack. What happens to it?
items.body: Export it and keep it. Kolabr does not require you to move history to start, because the usual first step is a single client channel running alongside what you already have. Most teams find the archive matters less than they expected once the current work has one home. The channel you open this week is the one you will be searching next year.

hero.title: Kolabr vs Basecamp
hero.lede: When a Basecamp project closes, so does the only place that held the conversation, and the next job for the same client starts from an empty page. Kolabr gives that client one channel that never ends, holding every request, every document and every answer you have ever given them. Here are the two side by side on structure, accountability, knowledge and price.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: A project ends. A client does not. Kolabr gives each relationship one channel that holds every request, every document and every conversation you have ever had with them, instead of an archive of finished projects you have to search through.

summary.title: The number that decides it
summary.body: Basecamp usually costs less, and this page says so. What a flat fee does not buy is a request with an owner and a clock on it, a wiki in the channel, or a relationship that outlives the project it started in.

statement.title: Most work does not have an end date
paragraphs: A project-shaped tool works beautifully for a thing with a beginning and an end: a launch, a build, a move. It starts to strain when the work is a relationship. A client you have had for six years is not a project. Neither is support, a retainer, a maintenance contract or a site you look after. Those produce a new project every few months and split the history across all of them.

A Kolabr channel is the relationship itself. The client joins once and stays. Work arrives inside it as requests, closes, and is still findable in two years alongside the wiki article that explains how you handled it. Nobody is re-invited, and nothing is archived away from the conversation that produced it.

sections.title: Tasks live inside the request, and die with it
paragraphs: Kolabr has tasks. What it does not have is a task manager. Every task belongs to the request that created it, is assigned to somebody, and disappears when that request is closed. There is no separate list to groom, no board that slowly fills with items nobody remembers agreeing to, and no second place to look for what is outstanding.

This is a deliberate limit. Free-standing to-do lists are easy to create and almost impossible to keep honest, and after a year they describe a version of the work that stopped being true months ago. Tying every task to a request means the list is always as current as the request it belongs to, and closing the request closes the loop.

items.body: No, and that is deliberate. Kolabr organises work by relationship rather than by project: a channel per client, site or department, which carries on after any single job ends. Inside it, work is tracked as requests with owners and deadlines. If you need Gantt charts and resource levelling, use a planning tool for that and run the client conversation in Kolabr.

items.title: Does Kolabr have tasks?
items.body: Yes, inside a request. A request can carry its own checklist of tasks, assigned and ticked off by the people working on it, and those tasks close when the request closes. What Kolabr deliberately does not offer is a free-standing task manager, because lists that float loose from the thing that caused them are how a tool fills up with work nobody remembers agreeing to.

items.title: Both offer free guests, so what is the difference?
items.body: Structure. In Basecamp a client is invited to a project and re-invited to the next one. In Kolabr a client has a channel that holds every piece of work you do together, so the history, the wiki and the open requests stay in one place across years rather than being split across archived projects.

items.title: What about ongoing work that never really ends?
items.body: This is the common reason firms outgrow a project-shaped tool. Support, retainers, maintenance and standing client relationships have no finish date, so they sit uneasily in something built around projects. A Kolabr channel has no end date, and requests come and go inside it.

items.title: Which is cheaper?
items.body: Usually Basecamp, and we would rather say so than dress it up. It charges one flat fee for the account, from $25 a month for up to twenty people and $59 with no limit on people, where Kolabr charges per user. What the fee buys is where they part: Kolabr covers requests with owners and response targets, a wiki in every channel, video calls and scheduled events, and organises around the client rather than the project. If a shared to-do list is all the structure your work needs, Basecamp is cheaper and will stay cheaper. The question is not which bill is smaller. It is whether a shared to-do list is the whole of what you owe a client.

items.body: Yes, and the usual approach is to stop creating new projects rather than migrate old ones. Open a channel for your busiest client, run the next piece of work there, and let the Basecamp archive stay readable for as long as you need it.

statement.title: The document is never where the conversation is

sections.title: A wiki small enough to stay true
paragraphs: Kolabr has a wiki in every channel, and it is deliberately not a company encyclopaedia. It holds what the people in that channel need: how a revision is issued, what counts as urgent, who signs what. Guests read it without a licence, and because its scope is one relationship it stays short enough that somebody actually maintains it.

It is that six hundred pages accumulate, nobody can tell which are current, and the honest answer to a question becomes asking a colleague instead. A wiki bound to one channel resists that, because its readers are the same handful of people every day.

items.title: Can Notion replace a chat tool?
items.body: Not really, and most teams do not ask it to. Notion carries comments on pages, but the running conversation of a working day happens somewhere else, which is why so many teams pay for Notion and a chat tool together. Kolabr puts the conversation, the request it produced and the article saying how that kind of work is handled in one channel.

items.title: Can I build a request tracker in Notion?
items.body: Yes, and people build good ones. The question is who maintains it. A Notion tracker is a database somebody designed, with views somebody configured and automations somebody keeps working, and it usually belongs to one person who eventually leaves. In Kolabr requests are part of the product: categories, owners, statuses, response targets and the channel’s own dashboard exist the moment you create it.

items.title: Both offer free guests, so what is the difference?
items.body: What a guest joins. In Notion a guest is shared individual pages. In Kolabr a guest joins a channel, which means the conversation, the open requests, the wiki and the calendar for that relationship, all at once. You are not deciding page by page what a client is allowed to see.

items.title: Does Kolabr have databases and custom views?
items.body: No, and that is deliberate. Kolabr has one structure that every channel shares: conversation, requests, wiki, events. You cannot model anything you like, and in exchange nobody has to design it, document it or repair it a year later when the person who built it has gone.

items.title: Which is cheaper?
items.body: On monthly billing Kolabr Pro is $10 and Notion Plus is $12, so we are the lower number; on annual terms Notion Plus is $10 and we are $8.50. Either way it is close, and the comparison changes once you count the chat tool you run alongside Notion and the time spent building and maintaining the trackers Kolabr includes. Price is rarely what decides this one. What decides it is who will own the tracker in two years.

items.title: Can we use Kolabr and Notion together?

Notion keeps the long-form internal knowledge it is already full of, and Kolabr runs client channels, where the conversation, the requests and the wiki for that relationship belong together. The channel wiki is for what a client or a new starter needs, not a company encyclopaedia.

hero.title: Kolabr vs ClickUp
hero.lede: In ClickUp a client can watch for free, and the moment they need to comment, approve or raise something they come out of a guest allowance and then onto your bill. So the people with the decisions stay outside it, and somebody on your team spends the week relaying for them. Kolabr guests post, raise requests, read the wiki and join calls, free, on every plan.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: A client who can only watch is not collaborating. In Kolabr every guest can post, raise a request, read the wiki and join a call, on every plan, at no cost.

summary.title: The number that decides it
summary.body: Per internal seat the two are close. The gap opens at the first client who has to approve something: ClickUp meters participating guests and then charges them as members, and Kolabr does not count them at all.

statement.title: A guest who can only look is not much of a guest
paragraphs: ClickUp’s free guests are view-only. The moment a client needs to comment, approve or change anything, they take a guest seat from an allowance that scales with how many paid users you have, and once that allowance is gone the next guest is billed as a full member. There is a further rule that catches people out: a guest whose email domain matches your workspace is converted to a paid member automatically.

Kolabr has one kind of guest and they participate fully. They raise requests, answer questions, read the wiki and join calls, and they are free on every plan. Nothing converts, nothing is metered, and nobody on your side has to think about who is worth a seat before inviting the person who has the answer.

sections.title: Tasks live inside the request, and die with it
paragraphs: Kolabr has tasks. What it does not have is a task manager. Every task belongs to the request that created it, is assigned to somebody, and disappears when that request is closed. There is no separate board to groom and no second place to look for what is outstanding, because what is outstanding for a client is the list of open requests.

This is a deliberate limit rather than a missing feature. Free-standing lists are easy to create and hard to keep honest, and a year in they describe a version of the work that stopped being true months ago. Tying every task to a request means the list is exactly as current as the request it belongs to.

hero.title: Kolabr vs Zendesk
hero.lede: Per-agent pricing makes you decide which colleagues are allowed to help, and a portal makes your client decide whether a question is worth logging in for. Across forty named accounts, both of those cost you more than the licence does. Kolabr keeps the owners, the categories and the clocks, and puts them in the channel your client is already in.

summary.title: The short version
summary.body: If your customers are strangers and there are thousands of them, buy a helpdesk. If they are named accounts you will still have in five years, the queue is the wrong shape and a channel is the right one.

summary.title: The number that decides it
summary.body: A helpdesk charges per agent, so every colleague who could answer is a budget decision. Kolabr is priced per person on your plan, and the client and their staff are guests at no cost, so nobody is rationed out of helping.

statement.title: A queue is the wrong shape for forty named clients
paragraphs: Helpdesk software is designed around a stranger with a problem. It is why there is a portal, a form and a set of macros: when the volume is thousands a month from people you will never meet again, structure at the front door is what keeps it survivable. That design is a poor fit when the person raising the request is the same practice manager you spoke to yesterday and will speak to every week for the next three years.

In Kolabr the request sits inside the relationship rather than in front of it. The client is already in the channel, so they type, and one step turns that message into a numbered request with a category, an owner and a response target. The thread is attached, the history is right there, and nobody had to log in to a second system to tell you something.

items.title: Is Kolabr a helpdesk?
items.body: No, and it is the comparison we are most careful about. A helpdesk is built for volume from people you will never meet: a portal, a queue, macros, deflection. Kolabr is built for named relationships that last years, where the client is in the channel with you and the request is one part of an ongoing conversation. If your support is thousands of tickets a month from strangers, a helpdesk is the right tool. If your support is forty accounts whose names you know, a queue throws away the thing that makes you worth keeping.

items.title: Why would a support team choose Kolabr instead?
items.body: Because not all support looks like a contact centre. A managed service provider with forty clients, a firm with named accounts, a supplier with a handful of large customers: in those, the people raising requests are the same faces every week, and putting a portal between you and them removes the context rather than organising it.

items.title: Do we pay per agent?
items.body: No. Kolabr is priced per person on your plan, and anyone in your company can be in a channel and answer a request. Nobody has to decide whether a colleague is worth an agent seat before letting them help, and the client and their staff are guests at no cost.

items.title: Do clients need to log into a portal?
items.body: No. They are in the channel, which is where they already talk to you. There is no separate system to learn, no password to forget and no moment where somebody gives up and sends an email instead.

items.title: Can we run both?
items.body: Yes, and some do. A helpdesk handles high-volume inbound from the general public while Kolabr runs the named accounts, where the relationship matters more than the queue. The two rarely overlap in practice, because they are shaped for different kinds of customer.

items.title: What does Kolabr include that a helpdesk plan charges for?
items.body: A wiki in every channel instead of a help centre you build and publish, full chat with direct messages, video calls, and scheduled events. One price, with no per-agent add-ons stacked on it.
